name: copy-paste-programming
intent: Records what Copy-Paste Programming costs: the same knowledge written down N times, so a requirement change is an N-part edit, a defect is an N-part fix, and the copies drift — the price is that the codebase's behaviour can only be changed by finding every copy, and there is no mechanism that tells you when you have missed one.
problem: Code is duplicated rather than abstracted, and each copy is then modified in place. The immediate cause is usually a rational trade: introducing an abstraction touches working code and risks changing existing behaviour, whereas copying is safe, fast and reversible.
context: The literature calls the technique copy-paste-modify — explicitly duplicating source code and adapting the duplicate for a new purpose — and the practice is pervasive: Laguë et al. found 6.4% to 7.5% of a large mature codebase to be exact or renamed clones, and Baxter et al. reported over 25% on other codebases once near-miss clones are counted. The motivation is well documented and not irrational: introducing a possibly complex abstraction into existing, working code alters behaviour operationally and risks inadvertent semantic changes, while copying avoids that risk entirely. That mismatch between what developers want (the study's informal poll found C++ developers prefer abstraction) and what they do is called the reuse discrepancy, and it is the honest description of why this happens. Fowler's framing is that duplication is number one on the stink parade — the same code structure in more than one place. Practically, the clone taxonomy matters: exact and renamed clones (types 1 and 2) are trivial to detect, but type-3 near-miss clones with nontrivial differences are the ones that matter and the ones that tools find hardest, and they are also the ones that evolve out of types 1 and 2.
benefits: The immediate, real benefit is safety: copying never changes existing working code, so a change cannot regress the behaviour that already worked. That is why the practice is so hard to argue away.

It is the right answer when the two pieces genuinely differ in more than a parameter, when a shared abstraction would need a configuration mechanism nobody wants to build, or when the duplication is a temporary artefact of a migration that will end.

Fowler notes that duplication is the most common form of structural debt and the easiest to fix mechanically — Extract Method is the first remedy in every catalog, because it is low-risk and mechanical.
The tools are mature, and unlike most refactorings, clone removal is partly automatable: merge tools for near-miss clones can propose the abstraction and have it accepted by maintainers.
It is also the mechanism by which the codebase gets large fast, which matters in a delivery-constrained project where shipping is the only thing that is measured.
tradeoffs: The cost is quantified and it is not small: cloning buggy code propagates the bug to every copy, and inconsistent clones have been shown to be a source of faults in maintenance studies.

Removal is not free and the tooling is honest about it — analysis of clone-merge approaches reports refactorable-clone rates of 6.2% to 33% depending on the detector and project, with no evidence offered that the resulting merges were acceptable to developers.

Abstraction has a cost and the cost is paid by the abstraction, not the copies. A shared helper that needs five parameters to accommodate five slightly-different call sites is worse than five short call sites, and the 'rule of three' heuristic exists because the judgement is genuinely uncertain below that.
The 'temporary' duplication is almost never temporary, because nothing enforces the retirement and the next change arrives first.

Clone detection has a precision/recall problem: type-3 clones with nontrivial differences are hard to detect, and clone groups that look similar may be genuinely different — which is why the merge tools ask the developer to choose the abstraction rather than inferring it.

Copying across files, packages or languages breaks the traceability between a copy and its origin, so the dependency between them is maintained by memory, and the MSR study of over 20,000 Eclipse users found cross-language copy-paste common enough that detection across languages is a separate research problem.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Performance and scalability are high because duplication is not a runtime property — the program does exactly what it did before, which is why the smell survives review. Extensibility is the worst axis, because the smell's whole cost is paid at the moment of the next change: a requirement that must be implemented in every copy has no single place to change. Reliability sits mid rather than low because each copy is individually correct; the risk is the drift between them, which shows up as an inconsistency defect rather than a crash.

participants.responsibility: The code the others were copied from, which is the only place that stays in the reader's mind as authoritative.
participants.notes: The origin's ownership is implicit: nothing in the code says which copy is the real one.

participants.responsibility: A duplicate that was then modified in place, producing a type-3 near-miss clone whose difference from the original is the only record of an intent.
participants.notes: The difference is where the design knowledge lives, and it is the part nobody reads.

participants.responsibility: The abstraction that should replace the copies, and the place the cost of over-abstraction would otherwise be paid.
participants.notes: The judgement about whether the copies share enough to warrant it is the whole difficulty of this smell.

use_cases: A bug fixed in one copy and left in the other, which is the highest-severity instance and the reason the practice is a smell rather than a style.
The logging concern copied into every module, where a change to the log format is a multi-file campaign.
A permission check pasted before every mutating endpoint, with one endpoint eventually missed.

Fowler's examples: the same expression in two methods of a class (Extract Method), in sibling subclasses (Extract Method then Pull Up Method), and the same logic in two unrelated classes (Extract Component).
Code generated by copying a template and adjusting the constants, where the constants are the design.
Cross-language duplication, where the same logic exists in a backend and a frontend because the boundary made sharing look impossible.
avoid_when: The two pieces differ in more than the parameters: if the shared version would need a configuration mechanism, two explicit implementations are clearer.
The duplication is a deliberate fork — the copies are intended to evolve independently, which is the case Kapser and Godfrey's work on non-harmful cloning identifies as legitimate.
The duplication is a temporary step in a migration that has a named owner and a retirement condition, recorded as such.
The abstraction would live in the wrong place: the shared code belongs to a boundary, not to either of the two sites that happen to need it now.
The two pieces are in separate deployed units or owned by separate teams, where a shared library is a coupling neither team wants.
Below the rule of three: two occurrences is often a coincidence rather than a pattern, and premature abstraction costs more than it saves.
pitfalls: Fixing the bug in one copy and shipping, which is the failure that makes duplication a reliability problem rather than only a maintenance one.
Extracting too eagerly: a shared function with five parameters and four optional flags is worse than the copies and harder to remove.
Compressing rather than unifying: rewriting the copies into a dense form first and then finding no two are alike.
Leaving the temporary duplicates behind after the migration completes, which is the same boat-anchor mechanism applied to a good decision.
Trusting a clone detector's output as a refactoring plan: type-3 clones differ in ways that may be intentional, and the merge tools ask a human to choose the abstraction for exactly that reason.

Ignoring that the copies carry different histories: the MSR work found developers' recollection of what was copied from where is short-lived, which is why the dependency has to be reconstructed rather than remembered.

related_patterns_notes.method-object: Extract Method is the first remedy in Fowler's catalog and the reason it recurs as a catalog pattern: a duplicated block becomes a method, and once extracted it is named, testable and shareable.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: When the duplicates are sibling subclasses doing the same steps with different bits, Extract Method then Pull Up Method is the named sequence, and Form Template Method is the fallback when they are similar but not identical.
related_patterns_notes.parameter-object: When the shared shape is the argument list rather than the body — several methods receiving the same five parameters — the duplicate is in the signatures, and a parameter object is the merge point.
related_patterns_notes.collecting-parameter: The same idea applied to a parameter threaded through a call chain: gathering it into an object removes the repeated plumbing without forcing the operations together.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy is the merge point when the duplicated code is a family of parallel conditionals over a kind — the copies become the strategies rather than being unified into one branch.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: Cross-cutting duplication is not a merge target: a concern copied into every function is a case for a decorator or interceptor, because it applies at many call sites and belongs to none of them.
related_patterns_notes.command: When the copies differ in what they do rather than in what data they use, a common command interface with per-copy implementations is the merge point and keeps the differences explicit.
related_patterns_notes.mapper: A mapper is the merge point for duplicated field-by-field conversion, which is the most common duplication in codebases with wire types.

anti_patterns: The partial bug fix: one copy patched and the others left, so the same defect exists in N places with different behaviour.
A cross-cutting concern (logging, auth, metrics, validation) inlined at every call site instead of applied once.
The 'temporary' duplicate that survives several releases because nothing enforces its retirement.
Over-abstracting the merge: a shared function whose parameter list and flags are more complex than the copies were.
The compressed rewrite: rewriting duplicated blocks into a denser form, after which it turns out no two are actually alike.
Copying across a boundary (backend/frontend, service boundary, language boundary) so the same rule exists in two places with no shared option.
Templates copied and adjusted with the adjustments recorded only in the diff, so the knowledge that the copies should stay in sync is in nobody's head.
Duplicated configuration or schema that looks like data rather than code and therefore is never scanned for duplication at all.
design_principles: Once and only once: any behaviour that exists in more than one place is a promise you will have to keep in all of them.
Put behaviour with the data it operates on: duplicated handling of the same data is usually a misplaced operation, and moving it there removes the duplication as a side effect.
Extract before you optimise: a duplicated block that is already a named method is a shared one, so extraction is the step that makes the duplication findable and safe to remove.
Abstraction has a cost and must earn it: the rule of three is a heuristic about when the shared form is cheaper than the copies, not a rule of law.
Cross-cutting concerns belong at a boundary, not at each call site: a concern that applies everywhere should be applied once by the framework rather than written N times.
best_practices: Measure before refactoring: run a clone detector on the whole tree, including tests and configuration, and rank clone groups by size and by how often they change together.
Treat type-3 (near-miss) clones as the real work — exact clones are usually caught in review, and near-misses are the ones that carry the design knowledge.

Use Fowler's ladder in order: Extract Method within a class, then Pull Up Method across sibling subclasses, Substitute Algorithm when the copies differ in method rather than text, Extract Component (Extract Class) when the copies are in unrelated classes.
Apply the rule of three as a trigger, not a gate: three real occurrences with the same shape is strong evidence; two is often coincidence.
When removing a cross-cutting copy, add the cross-cutting mechanism (decorator, interceptor, middleware, aspect) in the same change, or the next feature will copy it again.
Fix every copy of a bug, or the fix is not a fix — make the multi-file nature of a security or correctness fix visible in the commit.
Track temporary duplicates explicitly with an owner and a removal condition, the same discipline as any other deferred work.
Prevent recurrence with a just-in-time check: an editor or CI hook that flags a paste above a size threshold keeps the count from growing even when removal is scheduled separately.
Re-run the detector after each removal, because extraction often reveals the next group and because some clones only become detectable once one is gone.
sources: Roy and Cordy, 'Cleaning up copy-paste clones with interactive merging', Automated Software Engineering, 2018 — copy-paste-modify as an explicit form of reuse that developers prefer to introducing an abstraction into working code; the reuse discrepancy; clone rates reported by Laguë et al. (6.4%-7.5%, types 1-2) and Baxter et al. (over 25%, including near-miss clones); the need for human-chosen abstractions; and the refactorable-clone rates of 6.2%-33% reported for existing tools.

Chris Reichen, 'Copy and Paste Redeemed' — the case that copy-paste-modify can be substantially faster than manual abstraction while empirical evidence also shows it complicates maintenance and increases bug frequency; maintainers finding algorithmically created abstractions 'largely preferable to the existing duplicated code'.

Tarek Ahmed, Haoxiang Zhang, Weiyi Ren and Xin Xia, 'An Empirical Study of the Copy and Paste', MSR 2015 — over 20,000 Eclipse users and 20 months of usage data; over 75,000 copy-paste incidents across different programming languages; the relay pattern being frequent among IDE users; and the finding that developers' recollection of copy-paste history is short-lived.

Jonathan Edwards and Tomas Petricek, 'Interaction vs. Abstraction: Managed Copy and Paste' — the conflict between abstraction and the simplicity of copying, and a proposal to let the environment track copies and propagate changes on command rather than requiring the abstraction up front.

AlOmar et al., 'AntiCopyPaster 2.0: Whitebox just-in-time code duplicates extraction', 2024 — the observation that not all duplicate code should be refactored, the 78 structural and semantic metrics used to classify whether extraction is worthwhile, and the F-measure of 0.82 for the learned classifier.

Kim et al., IBM Research, 'Understanding Programmers' Copy and Paste Operations' — the taxonomy of copy-paste usage patterns; that C&P dependencies often reflect real design decisions worth preserving; that programmers deliberately delay restructuring until they have copied several times to discover the right level of abstraction; and that the absence of repetitive-editing support in the IDE increases the need for syntactic templates.

Martin Fowler, 'Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code' (Addison-Wesley, 1999) — duplicated code as number one on the stink parade, and the ladder of remedies: Extract Method, Pull Up Method, Form Template Method, Substitute Algorithm, Extract Component.

Rochkind Kapser and Michael Godfrey, 'Cloning considered harmful considered harmful' — the cases in which cloning is a beneficial design practice, including forking where copies are intended to evolve independently.
Roy and Cordy classify Type-1/2/3 clones using the Koschke taxonomy; Type-3 clones (nontrivial differences) are the ones that matter for maintenance.
